svg.aria-label: How to write ч: one unbroken stroke · 3 movements
svg.title: Writing ч
svg.desc: 3 frames; frame N shows movements 1 to N of ч (cyrillic), the movement being added drawn in ink over the finished letter, whose outline is read from _fonts/NotoSansCyrillic-Static.ttf. Stroke order after RussianIrina, ‘Learning Russian - Alphabet letters, handwriting’, lowercase ч demonstration, 09:24–09:28, YouTube, 5 February 2013 <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tqDLDfYoO2o>. Source note on variation: The native-teacher video presents all 33 Russian letters first in print and then in the classic handwritten form taught at school. In the 09:24–09:28 lowercase ч demonstration, the pen begins at the upper left, descends the short left stem to a middle join, turns through a narrow rounded bridge, rises to the top of the right stem, descends that full stem to the baseline, and curls into a small rising exit without lifting. The demonstrated school hand therefore uses one continuous pen-down run with zero intervening lifts: short left stem down, joined rise, long right stem down, then the curled exit. The bundled Noto Sans Cyrillic glyph is a printed ч-like form with a shorter straight left stem, a shallow rounded bowl, and a full-height straight right stem, without the narrow bridge, curled baseline, or exit join. This learner path preserves the source's short-stem-to-bowl-to-long-stem order and zero-lift evidence while fitting the printed outline: descend the short left stem, sweep through the shallow bowl, rise along the right stem, and descend the full right stem without lifting. Connected cursive restores the source's narrower bridge, curled baseline, and rising exit, and individual handwriting may round, narrow, widen, or slant the bowl and stems differently.
svg.text: How it is written — one unbroken stroke · 3 movements
